newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Officials begin probing Sao Paulo air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Officials begin probing Sao Paulo air disaster.

text.p: Federal authorities on Friday began probing what caused a Fokker-100 aircraft to come down in a densely populated residential area of Sao Paulo, killing at least 104 people.

All 96 people on board and at least eight people on the ground died on Thursday when TAM airlines' Flight 402 ploughed into the densely populated neighbourhood of Parque Jabaquara just 30 seconds after takeoff.

Officials in Brazil's Civil Aviation Department (DAC), which is responsible for investigating the accident, said they had recovered the Fokker's two black boxes with recordings of the pilot's last conversations with his crew and air controllers. They said a final report on the accident would be published within 90 days.

Witnesses at Congonhas airport, the domestic airport from which the 108-seat plane departed, said they saw the thrust reverser on the Fokker's right turbine activate automatically as the plane raced down the runway.

The thrust reverser, which is used on landing to help bring a plane to a stop, is designed to reverse the direction of the engine's air intake, creating aerodynamic resistance. Experts cited by Brazilian newspapers said involuntary activation of the device was highly unusual and the effect of having one of the plane's two engines pushing in the opposite direction could easily explain the crash.

"I saw the right engine's air brake open up. That's not normal and creates a very strange sound," Antonio Bueno, an aircraft mechanic at Congonhas airport, said. "The next time I looked, the plane took a dive and disappeared underneath a mushroom-shaped cloud."

Early on Friday, DAC officials collected the last pieces of the Fokker from a four-block area and took them to a TAM hangar for investigation. Fokker officials were expected to travel from Holland to help determine the cause of the crash.

Firefighters who helped retrieve the dead said the bent-over position of many of the victims suggested the plane's passengers had been aware of imminent danger. "Although the bodies were completely charred, one could see that they were bent over," Lt. Col. Leopoldo Correa Filho said.
Officials said Flight 402, which crashed less than a mile (1.6 km) from the end of the runway, never managed to climb above 90 feet (30 metres).

By Friday morning, only 30 of a total of 97 bodies at the city morgue had been positively identified, including those of an elderly woman who was travelling with her son and daughter. TAM officials assembled victims' familiy members at a hotel near the airport, where they were shown videos of the bodies to help speed identification.

The disaster shocked Brazil's business community, as the list of the dead included the names of many well-known banking and business executives. Citibank, Bank of Boston, Chase, Siemens, Parmalat, Coca-Cola and ABB Brown Boveri were among multinational corporations that had executives on board.
Unibanco, Brazil's second-largest financial institution, reported eight of its executives had been killed.

The early-morning TAM flight to Rio de Janeiro was a favourite among Brazilian business people who routinely shuttle between Rio and Sao Paulo on the same day. TAM, Latin America's fastest-growing regional carrier, was popular among business-class clients for its in-flight service.
Just three days ago, TAM's maverick president-owner, Comandante Rolim Adolfo Amaro, told a news conference, "The worst that could happen to us would be an aircraft accident."
TAM stock, which had risen more than 150 percent so far this year, plunged almost 15 percent after the accident.
